confidence_note: Old TR text cited COVID-19 vaccine falsehoods and deepfakes; a 2018 book cannot contain COVID-19, and the Cambridge Analytica/deepfake examples and the evolved-brain 'tribal leader' argument were not verified in the book, so all are removed. Kept only: the book's opening claim that clarity is power in a world flooded with irrelevant information; censorship by flooding people with disinformation and distractions (both from the publisher blurb); the widely quoted fake-news line (thousand people / one month versus a billion / a thousand years) from the post-truth chapter; and advice that reliable information is worth paying for (confirmed via a review, not the text). The echo-chamber advice is not confirmed and is omitted. No other quotes.
facts: The book opens with the claim that in a world deluged by irrelevant information, clarity is power.
Harari says censorship in the 21st century works not by blocking information but by flooding people with disinformation and distractions.

In the fake-news discussion he writes that when a thousand people believe a made-up story for one month, that is fake news, and when a billion people believe it for a thousand years, that is a religion.
He argues that fake news is old and that shared stories have long inspired people, often to good effect.
Among his practical advice on fake news: if you want reliable information, be ready to pay for it.
scene_details: a thousand people believing a story for one month
a billion people believing a story for a thousand years
a flood of disinformation and distractions
tension: Information is cheap and everywhere, yet knowing what to trust is harder; the flood is itself the problem.
opening_idea: Harari opens his book by saying that censorship today works by drowning people in noise rather than by hiding facts.

lessons.idea: With too much information around, the scarce skill is deciding what deserves your attention and trust, and good sources can cost time or money.
lessons.anchor: Harari's claim that clarity is power in a flood of information, and his advice to pay for reliable information.

reflect_final: Which source do you trust most for news that matters to you, and what makes you think it earns that trust?

use_cases.situation: A colleague forwards a dramatic claim to the team chat.
use_cases.move: Ask where it came from and who would have to be wrong if it were false, before anyone repeats it.

use_cases.situation: A relative shares a viral post at dinner.
use_cases.move: Say you want to check it first and suggest looking up one source that is paid to get facts right.

use_cases.situation: You scroll for news every morning without paying for any of it.
use_cases.move: Harari says reliable information may be worth paying for; pick one outlet that checks its facts and give it your first ten minutes instead of the feed.

pocket_idea: Harari: in a flood of information, censorship comes as noise, so choose a few sources worth paying for.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Harari says modern censorship does not hide facts, it buries them in noise.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Harari begins 21 Lessons by saying that in a flood of irrelevant information, clarity is power, and that censorship now works by flooding people with disinformation and distractions. On fake news he writes that a made-up story believed by a thousand people for a month is fake news, but believed by a billion for a thousand years it is a religion. His practical tip: reliable information is worth paying for.
